questionText: Which statement keeps task exposure, substitution potential and employment effect apart?

answerOptions.text: A high exposure value proves the same share of jobs goes
Exposure and substitution potential do not directly predict adoption or net employment
Once one core task is automatable, the whole occupation counts as abolished
The three terms name the same statistical quantity

explanation: The OECD Employment Outlook 2023 describes employment in occupations at high risk of automation, the IAB substitution potential the technically automatable share of core tasks. Neither is an adoption rate or job-loss forecast.

questionText: How do you get a defensible comparison for an AI-assisted task?

answerOptions.text: Take one time estimate without comparison or quality check
Same task with and without assistance; record time, errors, quality, rework
Generalise from one good demo to every occupation
Measure productivity by the volume of text produced

explanation: Only with the same task, quality criteria and documented rework can you see whether assistance saves time, merely shifts errors or adds review.

questionText: Which description fits practical AI literacy best?

answerOptions.text: Programming, training models, analysing data
Speaking English, using international AI tools, collecting certifications
Know purpose and limits, review output, mind data protection, responsibility, escalation
Spotting deepfakes, programming chatbots, maintaining databases

explanation: Article 4 of the AI Regulation requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting the AI literacy of their staff and other people they deploy. It does not guarantee a particular level for every individual.

answerOptions.text: The right to program AI systems yourself
Introducing or using technical equipment meant to monitor behaviour or performance
The right to train employees on AI tools
The right to reject every AI system outright

explanation: The works council's co-determination right applies where no statutory or collective-agreement rule exists. Without agreement, the conciliation committee can decide under Section 87(2).

questionText: What makes image, audio or video content a deepfake under Article 3(60) of the AI Regulation?

answerOptions.text: Elaborate manual editing by specialist graphic designers
AI generation or manipulation, resemblance to something existing, false appearance of authenticity
Only production by intelligence services with special hardware
Simply copying and blending existing material

explanation: All three must apply together, and the resemblance can concern people, objects, places, entities or events. The definition prescribes no particular technique or amount of reference material.

questionText: When does Article 50 of the AI Regulation start to apply?

answerOptions.text: From 2 February 2025
From 2 August 2026
From 1 January 2027
This duty has not been adopted yet

explanation: Providers of covered generative systems mark output in machine-readable form under paragraph 2; deployers disclose deepfakes visibly under paragraph 4, with exceptions. For systems on the market before 2 August 2026, paragraph 2 applies from 2 December 2026 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

questionText: What do you do first with a suspected deepfake?

answerOptions.text: Call the Federal Criminal Police Office and file a complaint
Forward it to everyone you know so they can check
Don't share it publicly; save source, time and evidence locally
Publish your own fact-check on social media

explanation: Every public share can widen the reach. Secure the source, check provenance and context, and only then choose the right reporting or contact route.

questionText: Which statement about Section 22 KUG is correct?

answerOptions.text: The right to publish works of art without a licence
The right to delete images made by AI
Distributing or publicly showing portraits needs consent; Section 23 sets exceptions
Protection for journalists doing undercover research

explanation: Section 23 sets the exceptions and, in paragraph 2, a balancing of interests. Section 22 KUG does not protect your voice on its own.

questionText: Which account of the COMPAS controversy is supported?

answerOptions.text: The system worked flawlessly and fairly for every group
ProPublica reported unequal error rates; Northpointe cited similar calibration per risk band
The system was technically defective and produced random results
It ran only in Florida and had no further effects

explanation: ProPublica found different error rates in the Broward County scores it examined; Northpointe countered with calibration. Where base rates differ, both fairness criteria generally cannot be met at once.

questionText: What did Gender Shades find for commercial gender classification?

answerOptions.text: Every system recognised faces with an error rate below 5 percent
Error rates differed only slightly between the four groups studied
Only older systems showed bias; modern ones are free of it
Lighter-skinned men at most 0.8 percent error, darker-skinned women up to 34.7 percent

explanation: Gender Shades tested binary gender classification, not identification through facial recognition, and measured substantial intersectional differences. It did not prove a training-data cause for each vendor.

questionText: Which statement about Article 22 GDPR is correct?

answerOptions.text: The right to have all your data deleted
Solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect
The right to inspect the AI system's source code
The right to switch the model off

explanation: Paragraph 2 holds exceptions; where a contract requires it or the person explicitly consented, paragraph 3 secures at least the right to human intervention, to state a view and to contest.

questionText: Which statement about deepfake detectors is correct?

answerOptions.text: Modern tools spot every deepfake with almost 100 percent accuracy
Depends on model, data and threshold; alone it proves nothing
Only public authorities have access to reliable detection tools
Reverse image search reliably spots every AI-generated image

explanation: Compression, cropping, post-processing, unknown generators and the threshold change what a result is worth. So you always check provenance and context.

questionText: Which tool splits videos into keyframes, triggers reverse searches and shows available metadata?

answerOptions.text: Any AI text detector
InVID/WeVerify (weverify.eu)
Google Lens
TinEye (tineye.com)

explanation: It generates keyframes, triggers reverse searches and shows available metadata, but it gives no verdict on truth.

questionText: Which statement about historical training data is precise?

answerOptions.text: AI developers deliberately build discriminatory systems
Training data are always too small, whatever their composition
Fair AI systems cannot be built at all
They can hold inequality; the effect also depends on model and deployment

explanation: Whether earlier selection or power structures turn into a harmful effect also depends on sample, labels, target, features, thresholds, testing and deployment.

questionText: Which statement about the EU AI Act and deepfakes is correct?

answerOptions.text: The EU AI Act bans all deepfakes with immediate effect
The EU AI Act has no rule on AI-generated content
Article 50 separates provider marking from deployer disclosure; recheck the complaint route
Deepfakes matter only to providers, not to individuals

explanation: Providers mark output in machine-readable form and deployers disclose deepfakes visibly, each with exceptions and transition rules. Under the KI-MIG, Article 85 complaints go to the Bundesnetzagentur unless a sector authority is competent.
